baptist.perseverance:
Baptists commonly speak of eternal security, or of being once saved always saved. The usual meaning is that a person who has truly trusted Christ as Saviour is kept by God's power and will not be lost. Many pulpits put the accent on Christ's finished work and on John 10: the sheep shall never perish. Assurance rests on the promise, not on a perfect record after conversion.

Not every Baptist says it the same way. Churches shaped by Calvinist confessions prefer perseverance of the saints: the truly regenerate will endure because God preserves them, and a life that finally abandons Christ is taken as evidence that the profession was never genuine. Other congregations warn that a believer can so wreck fellowship as to lose joy and usefulness without losing salvation itself. A smaller stream, often among Free Will Baptists, holds that a saved person may finally fall away. When Baptists differ here, they still treat the question as a family dispute about how God keeps His own, not as a denial that salvation is by grace through faith.
baptist.polity:
Baptist church government is congregational. Each local body of baptized believers is, under Christ, competent to receive members, call a pastor, elect deacons, handle its money, and discipline its own. No bishop, association, or convention has binding authority over a congregation that does not freely grant it. Associations and mission boards exist for cooperation, not for rule.

Congregational government does not mean that the pastor has no voice, or that the church is a pure democracy without Scripture. Most Baptists expect the pastor to lead by preaching and example, and the members to decide major matters in church conference. Some churches are elder-led congregational; others are strongly pastor-led. The shared conviction is that Christ is the only head of the church and that the keys, so far as men hold them, belong to the gathered congregation rather than to a hierarchy above it.
baptist.local_church:
The local church is the congregation of baptized believers in a place who covenant together to worship, observe the ordinances, hear the Word, and carry out the Great Commission. Baptists treat that body as autonomous. It does not need a bishop's leave to baptize, to celebrate the Lord's Supper, or to send missionaries. Sister churches may advise, and associations may withdraw fellowship, but they cannot unmake a church.

Because the local church is primary, membership matters. It is not a loose audience but a company of people who have professed faith, been baptized as believers, and placed themselves under the watchcare of that body. How strictly that is practiced varies from church to church, yet the ideal remains a regenerate, baptized, accountable congregation rather than a parish defined by geography or birth.
baptist.ordination:
Ordination among Baptists is the church's public recognition that a man has been called to gospel ministry and is fit to preach, baptize, and shepherd. A council of pastors and brethren from sister churches commonly examines the candidate on conversion, call, and doctrine, then the local church votes and lays on hands. The act does not confer a priestly character or an indelible office above the people. It sets a servant apart for work the congregation has already judged him able to do.

Practice varies. Some churches ordain only pastors; others also ordain deacons or missionaries. Some require seminary training; many independent churches do not. Women pastors are accepted in some Baptist bodies and refused in others. What is shared is that ordination is an act of the local church under Scripture, not a sacrament administered by a bishop in succession.
baptist.elders:
Baptist usage of elders and pastors is not uniform. In a great many churches the pastor is the preaching elder, and the word elder is rarely used. Other churches, especially those that read the New Testament more tightly on church office, recognize a plurality of elders who share oversight, sometimes distinguishing a teaching pastor from other elders.

Where Baptists do speak of elders, they mean overseers of the flock, not a higher clergy caste. They are to meet the qualifications of 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1, to labor in the Word, and to watch for souls. They remain members of the congregation that called them. The older Baptist pattern of a single pastor with a board of deacons is still widespread; the plurality-of-elders pattern has grown without replacing it.
baptist.deacons:
Deacons in Baptist churches are servants of the congregation, chosen to free the pastor for the ministry of the Word and prayer and to care for the practical and merciful work of the body. The model is Acts 6 and the qualifications of 1 Timothy 3. They are not a second house of rulers, though in some churches the deacon body functions as the main advisory board to the pastor.

How they are chosen and how much authority they hold differs widely. Some churches elect deacons for limited terms; others treat the office as standing. Some restrict the office to men; some Baptist bodies also have deaconesses or women deacons. The common thread is that the deacon is a recognized servant of the local church, not a priest and not, by office alone, the pastor of the flock.
baptist.priesthood_of_believers:
Soul competency and the priesthood of believers are near the center of Baptist speech. Soul competency means that each person stands before God without a human priest as mediator and is able, by the gospel and the Spirit, to answer God for himself. The priesthood of believers means that every regenerate member has access to God through Christ, may read the Scriptures, and shares in the church's worship and witness.

This is not a claim that every member is equally gifted to preach or that the church has no teachers. It is a refusal of a mediating priesthood and of any authority that would bind the conscience apart from Scripture. The same conviction underwrites believer's baptism, congregational government, and liberty of conscience. Baptists disagree about how far private judgment may run against the gathered church, but they agree that no bishop or state stands between the soul and Christ.
baptist.baptism:
Believer's baptism is the Baptist ordinance in which a person who has already professed personal faith in Christ is immersed in water in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. It is an act of obedience and a public confession, picturing the believer's union with Christ in death, burial, and resurrection. It does not wash away original sin in an infant, and it is not itself the new birth, though Churches of Christ and some others outside typical Baptist ranks treat immersion as the moment sins are remitted.

Most Baptist churches require baptism as a believer, usually by immersion, before membership and before the Lord's table. A minority will receive a person immersed as a believer in another evangelical church. Infant sprinkling is not accepted as baptism. The ordinance belongs to the local church, not to a diocese, and it follows conversion rather than producing it.
baptist.infant_baptism:
Baptists practice believer's baptism only. They do not baptize infants, because they read the New Testament pattern as hear, believe, repent, then be baptized. An infant cannot profess faith, so the rite administered to infants is not, in Baptist judgment, New Testament baptism. They often call their view credobaptism to mark the contrast with covenant or household baptism.

Children are welcomed, taught, and prayed for. Dedication services in many churches present an infant to the Lord without calling the act baptism. When a boy or girl later trusts Christ, that profession is tested as far as a church can test it, and then the person is immersed. Reformed Baptists still reject infant baptism even when they otherwise share a Calvinist reading of the covenant; they locate the covenant sign in those who give credible evidence of new birth.
baptist.mode_of_baptism:
The Baptist mode is immersion. The word baptize, as Baptists have long argued, means to dip or plunge, and the picture of burial and rising with Christ in Romans 6 and Colossians 2 fits a going down into the water and a coming up. Pouring and sprinkling are therefore not treated as the New Testament form, even when the candidate is a believer.

In practice nearly all Baptist baptisms are a single immersion of a professing believer in a baptistry or in open water. A church may, in rare cases of grave illness, face a hard pastoral choice, but the standard remains immersion. Mode is not a mere preference of style; it is part of what makes the ordinance the ordinance, which is why Baptists have historically declined to call infant pouring baptism at all.
baptist.sacraments:
Baptists prefer the word ordinances for baptism and the Lord's Supper. An ordinance is a rite Christ commanded the church to keep. It is not a channel that automatically confers saving grace, and Baptists do not number seven sacraments. The two ordinances belong to the gathered church of baptized believers.

Calling them ordinances rather than sacraments is meant to guard the gospel: sinners are justified by faith in Christ, not by a rite. That does not make the ordinances empty. They preach the gospel to the eyes, bind the church together, and call for self-examination. A few Baptist writers have been willing to say sacrament in an older, weaker sense of a holy sign, but the everyday vocabulary remains ordinance, and the everyday caution remains against treating the water or the table as the place where grace is created.
baptist.real_presence:
At the Lord's table most Baptists hold a memorial view. The bread and the cup are signs that show the Lord's death until He comes. Christ's body is in heaven; He is not localized in the elements. The blessing of the Supper is in remembering, proclaiming, and communing with the risen Christ by faith, not in a change of the substance of bread and wine.

Symbolic presence is the phrase some use for the same conviction: the signs point to Christ and the Spirit may make the remembrance precious, but the bread remains bread. Baptists therefore reject transubstantiation and also the Lutheran sacramental union. They still treat the table as holy and warn against eating unworthily. Frequency varies from weekly to quarterly. The shared insistence is that the Supper is a memorial ordinance for believers, not a repeated sacrifice and not a physical eating of Christ's flesh.
baptist.closed_communion:
Close communion, in Baptist use, means that the Lord's table is for baptized believers, and often specifically for those baptized as believers by immersion, sometimes only for members of that local church. The aim is to keep the ordinance tied to the same gospel and the same church order as baptism.

Practice is not uniform. Some churches invite all who are saved and have been immersed as believers, which many still call close rather than strictly closed. Others restrict the table to their own membership. Open communion, inviting all who profess faith regardless of baptism, has grown in some Baptist conventions and is resisted in others as loosening church discipline. The older Baptist instinct is that those who sit at the table should already have confessed Christ in the water in the way that church understands baptism.
baptist.altar_call:
The invitation, or coming forward, is a common close to a Baptist preaching service. After the gospel is preached, the pastor calls on hearers to respond: to trust Christ, to seek baptism and membership, or to make a public rededication. Those who come are met at the front, spoken with, and often presented to the church.

Baptists do not all agree that an invitation is required by Scripture. Some churches never give one and trust the Spirit to work through the Word without a walk down the aisle. Others treat the invitation as almost part of the sermon. Even where it is used, thoughtful Baptists insist that walking forward does not save. Faith in Christ saves. The invitation is only a public way to own that faith and to place oneself under the church's care.
baptist.church_and_state:
Separation of church and state and soul liberty are Baptist convictions with a long memory. The church must not be an arm of the magistrate, and the magistrate must not coerce faith, fund a preferred pulpit, or punish dissent in religion. Soul liberty means that God alone is Lord of the conscience, so civil power should not compel a creed.

This is not a claim that Christians should be silent in public life, nor that the state has no moral interest in justice. It is a claim that baptism, membership, discipline, and doctrine belong to the church, not to the crown or the legislature. Early Baptists paid for that view in jail and in fines. Modern Baptists still argue about how far a Christian citizen should press biblical morals in law, but the institutional line remains: the church is a voluntary body of believers, and the state is not its head.
baptist.ordination_of_women:
Baptists do not speak with one voice about women pastors. Some conventions and many independent churches read the pastoral epistles as limiting the office of pastor-elder to qualified men, while encouraging women in a wide range of other ministries. Other Baptist bodies ordain women to the pastorate and treat the restriction as cultural rather than abiding.

Because each congregation is autonomous, the dispute is settled locally more than by a single hierarchy. A church that calls a woman as pastor is still, in Baptist terms, a Baptist church if it holds believer's baptism and congregational order; a church that will not is not, in its own mind, thereby rejecting the priesthood of believers. The argument is over office and order, not over whether women may pray, teach other women and children, or serve. Visitors should not assume from the word Baptist which practice they will find.
